taxCredits.name: Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit
taxCredits.status: ended — not allowed for property placed in service (or expenditures made) after Dec. 31, 2025; 2025 work is still claimed on 2025 returns (Form 5695)
taxCredits.whatChanged: Public Law 119-21 (signed July 4, 2025), Sec. 70505, moved the credit's end date from Dec. 31, 2032 to Dec. 31, 2025 (the IRA had extended it through 2032). It also rewrote the oil furnace/boiler definition. IRS FAQ FS-2025-05 (Aug. 21, 2025): 'The credit will not be allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025.' Because of the early termination, manufacturers no longer need to file periodic written reports, though the QMID rule applied to 2025 property.
taxCredits.law: Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72 (July 4, 2025) — the reconciliation law commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — Sec. 70505, amending 26 U.S.C. 25C. Current text: 'This section shall not apply with respect to any property placed in service after December 31, 2025.'
taxCredits.lastEligible: Property placed in service on or before Dec. 31, 2025 (statute: not allowed 'after December 31, 2025'). Note: the IRS 25C page uses both 'through December 31, 2025' and 'before December 31, 2025'; the statute and FS-2025-05 use 'after December 31, 2025'.
taxCredits.amountsWhenAvailable: For 2023-2025: 30% of qualified costs. Annual cap $1,200 for efficiency property and improvements, with sub-limits: exterior doors $250 each / $500 total; windows and skylights $600; home energy audits $150; residential energy property (e.g., central AC, gas/propane/oil water heaters meeting the CEE top tier) up to $600 per item. Separate annual cap of $2,000 for qualified heat pumps, heat pump water heaters, biomass stoves and boilers. No lifetime limit; nonrefundable. Property placed in service in 2025 required the manufacturer's QMID on the return.
taxCredits.auditCredit: Up to $150 per year for a home energy audit of the main home (within the $1,200 cap). From 2024 the audit had to be done by, or under the supervision of, a qualified home energy auditor certified through a DOE-recognized Qualified Certification Program, with a signed written report giving the auditor's name and EIN/TIN, an attestation of certification and the program's name (IRS Notice 2023-59). It does NOT apply to audits paid for or done after Dec. 31, 2025: IRS instructions for 2025 and draft 2026 Form 5695 say the credit can't be claimed for expenditures or property placed in service after Dec. 31, 2025. An audit done in 2025 is claimed on the 2025 return.
taxCredits.notes: IRS 'One, Big, Beautiful Bill provisions' page (now titled 'Working Families Tax Cuts', updated Oct. 2, 2026): 25C 'Not allowed for any property placed in service after Dec. 31, 2025.' That page groups the home credits under 'Sections 70505-70507', but the enacted text puts the 45L change in Sec. 70508 (Sec. 70507 is the 179D commercial deduction). DOE still maintains its list of qualified auditor certification programs, with a banner noting P.L. 119-21 changed the credits.

overview.summary: STATUS IN 2026. The two Inflation Reduction Act rebate programs still exist and are funded: HOMES (IRA Sec. 50121, 42 U.S.C. 18795; $4.3 billion, available through Sept. 30, 2031) and the high-efficiency electric home rebate program (IRA Sec. 50122, 42 U.S.C. 18795a; $4.275 billion to states/territories plus $225 million to tribes, through Sept. 30, 2031). They are run by state energy offices, so availability depends entirely on the state. DOE's program page (modified July 8, 2026) says only that 'Home Energy Rebates are now available in select states' and that 'Additional details on active state, territory or Tribal rebate programs are coming soon.' DOE no longer publishes a current state-by-state status list: its old consumer status map (energy.gov/save/rebates) shows 'Last updated 04/09/2024' and returned HTTP 404 to a direct request on Oct. 12, 2026. FEDERAL CHANGES SINCE 2025. (1) Executive Order 14154 (Jan. 20, 2025), Sec. 7(a), ordered agencies to 'immediately pause the disbursement of funds appropriated through the Inflation Reduction Act'; several states report their plans then sat with DOE (Utah, page dated July 2025: DOE 'has not approved the application from Utah, nor those from numerous other state energy offices'; Montana paused planning in February 2025). (2) Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025) did NOT rescind HOMES (50121) or the electric rebate program (50122); Sec. 50402(b) rescinded only the unobligated balances of Sec. 50123, the $200 million state contractor-training grants, among other DOE programs. (3) DOE Program Notices 26-1 (HOMES) and 26-2 (HEEHR), effective May 29, 2026 and announced June 1, 2026, rewrote the rules: the names changed back to the statutory 'Home Owner Managing Energy Savings (HOMES)' and 'High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebates (HEEHR)' (replacing 'Home Efficiency Rebates' and 'Home Electrification and Appliance Rebates'/HEAR); the Justice40 requirement to reserve 40% of funds for low-income households, Community Benefits Plans and disadvantaged-community mapping were removed (HOMES keeps the statutory $200 contractor payment per home in a disadvantaged community); HEEHR no longer allows fuel switching — DOE now allows rebates only 'for upgrading HVAC and appliances only from existing electric equipment to more efficient electric equipment' (new construction still allowed), even though the statute's definition lists purchases made 'to replace a nonelectric appliance'; homes must get insulation and air sealing before heating/cooling upgrades unless already at a state-set level; consumer protection plans became 'Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Mitigation Plans' with Treasury 'Do Not Pay' contractor vetting; ENERGY STAR became optional for HOMES; several inspection and paperwork requirements were dropped; and if DOE does not respond within 30 days of final Blueprint feedback, a state may launch. Launched programs had three months to comply (states cite Aug. 31 or Sept. 1, 2026); reservations approved earlier may still be paid; states not yet launched must align before launching and many are now resubmitting (e.g., Maryland resubmitted Sept. 30, 2026; Virginia and Kentucky are updating documents). Program Notice 26-3 covers tribal HEEHR, whose application deadline was reopened to Dec. 11, 2026. HOW MANY STATES HAVE LAUNCHED. The Building Performance Association (June 2026) counts twelve states plus DC as launched: AZ, CA, CO, GA, IN, ME, MI, NC, NM, NY, RI, WI and DC; 55 states and territories applied (all but South Dakota). Rhode Island said in May 2026 it was 'one of only 12 states in the U.S. with active HEAR Programs.' Checking state pages on Oct. 12, 2026: at least one pathway is taking applications in 10 states plus DC — NY (HEAR via EmPower+), NC (both), GA (HOMES only; HEAR paused, reopening October 2026 with limited measures), CA (HEEHRA multifamily only; single-family fully reserved since Feb. 24, 2026), MI (both; new income-qualified applications paused in five districts), WI (both), NM (HEAR), IN (both), ME (HEAR for new affordable multifamily and mobile homes only), RI (HEAR; HOMES for multifamily launched Sept. 23, 2026) and DC (inside DCSEU's AHEP/AHRA programs). Colorado's single-family HEAR opened Nov. 13, 2025 and closed Aug. 1-2, 2026 after its funds ran out; West Virginia is in a pilot phase with a waitlist; Arizona could not be checked. The remaining states have not launched, according to their own pages or, where no state page could be checked (AR, LA, MA, MS, NE, NH, OH), according to BPA's June 2026 map.

weatherization.summary: WHAT IT IS: DOE's Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP) pays for energy-efficiency work in low-income homes through state agencies and local providers. DOE says it serves about 32,000 homes a year with DOE funds and that households save on average $372 or more a year; more than 7.2 million families have been served since 1976. FUNDING STATUS 2026: Funded, not eliminated. Public Law 119-74 (H.R. 6938, signed Jan. 23, 2026) provided FY2026 money; DOE's Weatherization Program Notice 26-2 (July 9, 2026) lists $329,000,000 for the Retrofit program, $10,000,000 for training and technical assistance and $30,000,000 for the Weatherization Readiness Fund (total $369,000,000), with Program Year 2026 state allocations; WPN 26-1 (same date) states the Retrofit figure as $328 million; the two notices also differ on availability (WPN 26-2: FY2026 funding 'through September 30, 2026'; WPN 26-1: 'through September 30, 2027'). FY2027 began Oct. 1, 2026 under a continuing resolution (Public Law 119-103, signed Sept. 2, 2026) that funds programs at FY2026 rates through Dec. 11, 2026. In July 2025 DOE released $325 million in WAP funds plus $30 million in Readiness funds and rescinded WPN 22-10, which had required counting the social cost of carbon and other non-energy benefits in cost-effectiveness tests. ELIGIBILITY: Federal rule (10 CFR 440.22) — household income at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines; or a member who received cash assistance under Social Security Act Title IV or XVI (e.g., TANF, SSI) in the previous 12 months; or, if the state elects, LIHEAP eligibility (which can use 60% of state median income) as long as the standard is at least 200% of poverty. With the 2026 HHS guidelines (effective Jan. 13, 2026: $15,960 for one person, $33,000 for four in the 48 states and DC), 200% is $31,920 for one person and $66,000 for four (as published by Pennsylvania's WAP). DOE's own income-guidelines page still shows the 2025 figures ($31,300 / $64,300 at 200%). WHAT IT COVERS: Work follows an energy audit; DOE requires that only cost-effective measures consistent with the audit are installed, that health and safety issues are treated, and that 100% of units are inspected (WPN 26-1); the program's stated purpose gives special attention to the elderly, people with disabilities and children. The Program Year 2026 average spending limit is $8,813 per home (renewable measures up to $4,436 within that average; no renewable electricity-generation technologies are approved). The Readiness Fund pays for repairs (structural, health and safety) that would otherwise defer a home. HOW TO APPLY: Contact your state weatherization administrator and local provider — DOE: 'To apply for WAP assistance, first identify your state weatherization administrator and reach out to them.' Steps: determine eligibility, identify the local provider, complete its application, prepare for the work.

liheap.summary: LIHEAP (HHS Administration for Children and Families) helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills, avoid shutoffs and make energy-related repairs; states may spend up to 15% (25% with a waiver) on low-cost weatherization. Eligibility under federal law: households receiving TANF, SSI, SNAP or certain veterans' benefits, or with income not above the greater of 150% of the poverty level or 60% of state median income (states set the exact limits; they cannot exclude households below 110% of poverty). FY2026: the program was funded despite a proposal to eliminate it. ACF released $3,713,859,933 on Nov. 28, 2025 (90% of continuing-resolution funds plus $100 million of IIJA supplemental money) and a final $421,540,067 on Apr. 17, 2026 under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148). NEADA describes the FY2026 total as $4.045 billion, $20 million more than the prior year. Staffing: HHS laid off the entire federal LIHEAP staff on Apr. 1, 2025, and NEADA reported in February 2026 they had not been rehired. FY2027: the Administration's FY2027 budget again proposed zeroing out LIHEAP; FY2027 began under a continuing resolution (P.L. 119-103, through Dec. 11, 2026). In a Sept. 17, 2026 letter, senators said the CR requires HHS to distribute at least 90% of LIHEAP allotments by Nov. 1, 2026 (I did not find that clause in the CR text I reviewed). Separately, P.L. 119-21 Sec. 10103 now limits the SNAP standard utility allowance that is triggered by receiving energy assistance to households with an elderly or disabled member. How to apply: through the state or local LIHEAP office; ACF points to energyhelp.us and the National Energy Assistance Referral line, 1-866-674-6327. ACF warns that LIHEAP does not give grants directly to individuals and does not charge a fee; such offers should be reported to the HHS fraud hotline (1-800-447-8477).

energyStar.summary: ENERGY STAR survived and is moving from EPA to DOE. In May 2025 EPA's FY2026 Budget in Brief listed the Atmospheric Protection program, which housed ENERGY STAR, among 'Programs Proposed for Elimination' ($108.4 million to $0), and trade press reported the administration sought to wind the program down; more than 1,200 organizations lobbied to keep it. Congress instead funded it: Public Law 119-74 (H.R. 6938, signed Jan. 23, 2026) requires that, of EPA's Environmental Programs and Management account, 'not less than $33,024,000 is to carry out the Energy Star Program' — reported as the first time Congress set a mandatory annual level. On Mar. 3, 2026 DOE and EPA signed a 10-year Memorandum of Agreement making DOE 'the lead Federal agency for the ENERGY STAR Program' and starting a transfer of primary management (partnership agreements, trademarks, IT systems). The Transition Plan was finalized Aug. 28, 2026; it targets moving the website, Portfolio Manager and Product Finder hosting to DOE before July 2027 and completing the transition within a year of the plan. DOE describes ENERGY STAR as a joint EPA-DOE program whose leadership is 'transitioning from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to the U.S. Department of Energy'. The FY2027 budget again proposes eliminating EPA's Office of Atmospheric Protection (Facilities Dive, Apr. 2026). For homeowners: energystar.gov, including the Rebate Finder (search by ZIP code), remains online. Note that DOE's 2026 rules made ENERGY STAR certification optional in HOMES rebate programs.

homeEnergyScore.summary: WHAT IT IS: DOE's Home Energy Score, 'developed by DOE and its national laboratories', rates a home's expected energy use on a 1-10 scale (like a miles-per-gallon rating; 5 = average US home, 10 = top 10%). It is an 'asset rating' based on about 40 data points about the envelope, systems and size collected in a walk-through of under an hour; it ignores occupant behavior and comes with cost-effective upgrade recommendations (payback within 10 years) and a 'score with improvements'. Single-family homes, townhouses and duplexes can be scored; multifamily and mobile homes cannot. 2026 STATUS: The program continues on DOE's Better Buildings Solution Center (homeenergyscore.gov redirects there), with a ZIP-code Find an Assessor tool and 22 listed partners (e.g., ASHI, BPI, InterNACHI, Earth Advantage, Pearl Certification, Oregon Department of Energy, City of Portland, Energize Connecticut, Focus on Energy, PSEG Long Island, New Jersey Natural Gas, South Carolina Energy Office, StopWaste, City of Fort Collins). DOE does not set fees; prices vary and the Score is often bundled with an audit or home inspection. WHO CAN PROVIDE IT: Home Energy Score Certified Assessors, who must hold an accepted credential (e.g., BPI BA/EP/HEP Energy Auditor/QCI, RESNET HERS Rater/RFI, ASHI Certified Inspector, InterNACHI Home Energy Inspector, AEE CEA/CEM, ICC residential inspector, LEED, NATE, CalCERTS/CHEERS raters), work through a DOE partner, pass an 8-12 hour simulation training and exam, score a first home with a mentor, and have 5% of homes re-scored for quality assurance. WHERE IT IS REQUIRED OR USED: Portland, Oregon requires sellers of most homes publicly advertised for sale to get a Score and Report before listing and to show it in all ads and at showings (ordinance adopted Dec. 14, 2016, City Code 17.108; reports reusable up to eight years; exemptions for financial distress or uninhabitable homes; free scores for sellers at or below 80% AMI). The Oregon Department of Energy oversees all Home Energy Score providers in Oregon and verifies assessor training for state licensing. Ann Arbor, Michigan adopted a Home Energy Rating Disclosure (HERD) ordinance for home sellers, reported in effect from Mar. 12, 2024 with a $500 fine and free city assessments (CBS Detroit, 2024; current status not re-verified). Utilities and agencies such as Energize Connecticut, Focus on Energy (WI), PSEG Long Island, Columbia Water & Light (MO), EWEB (OR) and Fort Collins' Epic Homes offer the Score voluntarily. Mortgage links: Freddie Mac GreenCHOICE requires a HERS report, DOE Home Energy Score report or comparable audit when energy/water improvements exceed $6,500; DOE says Fannie Mae and FHA products also reference the Score.

credentials.name: RESNET HERS Rater (Home Energy Rater)
credentials.certifiedBy: Residential Energy Services Network (RESNET); certification is issued by a RESNET-accredited Rating Provider
credentials.whatTheyDo: Inspects and tests homes and produces a HERS Index score under RESNET standards (reference home = 100, net-zero = 0); onsite tests typically include blower door and duct leakage testing. Most often used for new construction, ENERGY STAR and code compliance, but recognized for 25C audits (2024-2025), FHA Energy Efficient Mortgages and Home Energy Score assessor eligibility. Candidates pass a national online exam and complete five supervised ratings.
credentials.notes: The finder lists RESNET member rating companies and is not a complete list of raters; individual certification can be checked at https://www.hersindex.com/rater-verification/.

auditCosts.freeOrDiscounted: Utility and state efficiency programs commonly pay for most or all of an assessment. Verified 2026 examples: Mass Save (Massachusetts) offers 'a no-cost Mass Save Home Energy Assessment'; Energize Connecticut's Home Energy Solutions visit carries a $40 copay effective Apr. 1, 2026 and includes a blower-door test, up to seven hours of air sealing and a written report — about $1,000 in services on average — and is no-cost for households under 60% of state median income; Minnesota's Home Energy Squad (CenterPoint Energy and Xcel Energy) charges $100 for an Energy Planner visit (pre-2000 homes) or $70 for an Energy Saver visit, free for income-qualified households under 80% AMI. Low-income households can get an audit plus upgrades through the Weatherization Assistance Program, which state offices describe as provided at no cost (e.g., Vermont DPS: WAP 'provides weatherization and electrification services at no cost to low-income households'). Inside the new federal HOMES rebate programs, the required assessment may carry a fee (Georgia warns of possible assessment costs; Wisconsin's HOMES offers low-income households up to $500 toward it). The federal $150 audit tax credit (25C) ended for audits after Dec. 31, 2025.
auditCosts.notes: No DOE, EPA or HUD page found states a national typical price range for a home energy audit; DOE's Home Energy Score FAQ says 'DOE does not dictate Home Energy Score fees, so the price varies throughout the country.' DOE Energy Saver describes what a professional assessment includes (room-by-room review, utility bills, often a blower door test and thermographic scan) but gives no cost. Commercial cost guides could not be retrieved. Typical range left null rather than estimated.

otherFederal.name: FHA Energy Efficient Mortgage (EEM)
otherFederal.summary: HUD/FHA lets a borrower add the cost of cost-effective energy improvements to an FHA-insured purchase or no-cash-out refinance (203(b), 203(h), 203(k); one- to four-unit homes, condos, manufactured housing). Requires a home energy assessment by a BPI Building Analyst Professional, BPI HEP Energy Auditor, RESNET Home Energy Rater or a state/locally qualified auditor, with a report no more than 120 days old. Maximum energy package: the lesser of the cost-effective amount or 5% of the lowest of the Adjusted Value, 115% of the area median single-family price, or 150% of the national conforming loan limit. (Handbook 4000.1, EEM section dated Apr. 29, 2019; handbook last revised Aug. 12, 2026.)

otherFederal.name: FHA weatherization financing and 203(k) rehabilitation loans
otherFederal.summary: FHA's weatherization option finances energy-related weatherization items with a purchase or refinance: up to $2,000 without a separate value determination, $3,500 with an FHA roster appraiser's value determination, or more with an appraiser determination plus an ICC inspection; can be combined with an EEM. The Limited 203(k) covers minor, nonstructural repairs up to $75,000 in total rehabilitation costs.

otherFederal.name: Fannie Mae HomeStyle Refresh (former HomeStyle Energy)
otherFederal.summary: Conventional purchase or refinance that can include energy and water efficiency, resiliency and cosmetic improvements — up to 15% of the as-completed appraised value, up to 97% LTV; can pay off existing PACE or other energy-improvement debt. The former HomeStyle Energy URL now shows HomeStyle Refresh.

otherFederal.name: Freddie Mac GreenCHOICE Mortgages
otherFederal.summary: Finances energy and water efficiency improvements with a purchase or no-cash-out refinance — up to 15% of the 'as completed' value. Requires a HERS report, DOE Home Energy Score report or comparable audit unless basic improvements total $6,500 or less.

otherFederal.name: USDA Section 504 Single Family Housing Repair Loans & Grants
otherFederal.summary: USDA Rural Development program for homeowners who occupy their home, cannot get affordable credit elsewhere and meet county low/very-low income limits: loans up to $40,000 at 1% fixed for 20 years to repair, improve or modernize, and grants up to $10,000 (lifetime; age 62+ and very-low income) to remove health and safety hazards; combined maximum $50,000; grants repaid if the home is sold within three years. Applications accepted year-round at local Rural Development offices; approval depends on local funding (page modified Oct. 1, 2026).
